title: Ir vs Venir: Go or Come in Spanish?
seo_title: Ir vs Venir: Go or Come in Spanish?
meta_description: Ir vs venir: why Spanish says “ya voy” when English says “I’m coming”. The location rule, examples, invitations, common mistakes and a quick quiz.
excerpt: Why “I’m coming!” is ¡Ya voy! in Spanish, and the simple rule behind it.

image_plan.caption: Ir: away from where you are.

images.caption: Ir: away from where you are.

body_html:
Ir vs venir looks easy (“go” and “come”) until you answer the door in Spanish. When someone knocks, English says “I’m coming!”, but Spanish says ¡Ya voy!, literally “I’m going!”. The reason is that Spanish chooses between ir and venir strictly by the speaker’s location: venir means movement toward where the speaker is, and ir means movement anywhere else.

Quick answer
  • Venir = come, toward where the speaker is: Ven aquí.
  • Ir = go, toward anywhere else, including the listener: ¡Ya voy!
  • “I’m coming to your house” is Voy a tu casa.
  • Ya vengo means “I’ll be right back”, not “I’m coming”.
{{toc}}

Ir vs venir: the core rule

VenirIr
DirectionToward the speaker’s locationToward any other place
Englishto cometo go (and sometimes “to come”)
Example¿Vienes a mi casa? (said at home)Voy a tu casa. I’m coming to your place.

English lets you “come” to where the listener is. Spanish doesn’t: if you are not moving toward your own location, it is ir. The RAE dictionary defines venir as moving toward the place where the speaker is.

The classic mistake: “I’m coming!”

  • Someone calls you to dinner: ¡Ya voy! (not ¡Ya vengo!)
  • Your friend is waiting outside: Voy en cinco minutos. I’ll be there in five minutes.
  • On the phone: ¿Vas a venir a la fiesta? — Sí, voy. Are you coming to the party? — Yes, I’m coming.

And the opposite: Ya vengo means “I’ll be right back”, because you will return to where you are now.

{{image:2}}

Invitations: when venir is right

Venir works when the destination is the speaker’s place, or a place associated with the speaker, like their party:

  • ¿Quieres venir a cenar a casa? Do you want to come over for dinner? (The speaker’s home.)
  • ¿Vienes conmigo al cine? Are you coming with me to the movies? (venir con = come along with the speaker.)
  • Ven a mi boda. Come to my wedding.

When the destination belongs to someone else: ¿Vas a ir a la boda de Ana? Are you going to Ana’s wedding?

Conjugation note

Both verbs are irregular. Ir: voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van; past fui, fuiste, fue. Venir: vengo, vienes, viene, venimos, venís, vienen; past vine, viniste, vino. Commands: ve / vete (go / go away) and ven (come).

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Real conversations

At home

  • Mom: ¡La comida está lista! ¡Ven a la mesa! (Food’s ready! Come to the table!)
  • You: ¡Ya voy, mamá! (Coming, Mom!)

Making plans

  • A: ¿Vienes a mi casa esta noche? Vamos a ver una película. (Are you coming to my place tonight? We’re watching a movie.)
  • B: ¡Sí! Voy después del trabajo. ¿Llevo algo? (Yes! I’ll come after work. Shall I bring anything?)

Notice ¿Llevo algo?: the same location logic applies to {{link:llevar-vs-traer|llevar vs traer}}.

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrectWhy
¡Ya vengo! (meaning “coming!”)¡Ya voy!You move toward the listener, not yourself
Vengo a tu casa mañana.Voy a tu casa mañana.Their house isn’t your location
¿Vas a mi fiesta? (the host asking)¿Vienes a mi fiesta?The host’s party counts as “here”
Voy de México.Vengo de México. / Soy de México.Origin uses venir de or ser de
{{image:3}}

Ir vs venir on the phone and by message

Phone calls and texts are where learners slip most, because the “here” is less obvious. The rule still holds: think about where you are as you speak.

  • Your friend is at the café, you are at home: Voy para allá. I’m on my way there.
  • You are at the café, your friend is at home: ¿Vienes o no? Are you coming or not?
  • You are both going to a third place: ¿Vas a ir al concierto? Are you going to the concert?
  • You are already there and want them to join: Ven, que está muy bien. Come, it’s really good.

A useful related phrase is Voy para allá or, in Latin America, Voy en camino (I’m on my way). In Mexico you will also hear Ahorita voy, which can mean anything from “right now” to “in a while”.

Venir with past and future

The same logic applies in every tense. ¿Por qué no viniste ayer? (Why didn’t you come yesterday?) is said by someone who was at the place. ¿Por qué no fuiste? (Why didn’t you go?) is said by someone who wasn’t there either. Listening for that difference tells you a lot about where the speaker was.

Useful expressions

  • ¿Cómo te va? How’s it going?
  • ¡Vamos! Let’s go! / Come on!
  • Ir a + infinitive: near future, Voy a estudiar. I’m going to study.
  • Venir bien: to suit, ¿Te viene bien el lunes? Does Monday suit you?
  • ¿A qué viene eso? What’s that about? / Why do you say that?

For more pairs that depend on perspective, see {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}. You might also like {{link:salir-vs-irse|salir vs irse}}, another pair about movement.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Ir vs venir comes down to one fixed point: where the speaker is. Moving there is venir; moving anywhere else is ir. So next time someone knocks, answer like a native: ¡Ya voy!

faq.q: How do you say “I’m coming!” in Spanish?
faq.a: ¡Ya voy! Spanish uses ir because you are moving toward the other person, not toward your own location.
Ya vengo means “I’ll be right back”, because you will return to where you are now.

faq.q: Is it vienes or vas when inviting someone to my house?
faq.a: Vienes, because your house is your own location: ¿Vienes a mi casa esta noche?

questions.q: Someone knocks at your door. You shout: ¡Ya ___!
questions.explain: You are moving toward the other person, so Spanish uses ir.

questions.q: You invite a friend to your house: ¿___ a cenar el sábado?
questions.explain: Your house is your location: venir.

questions.q: Mañana ___ a tu oficina a las diez. (I’ll come to your office.)
questions.explain: Their office isn’t where you are: ir.

questions.q: You step out for a minute: Ya ___. (I’ll be right back.)
questions.explain: Ya vengo means you will return here.

questions.q: ¿Te ___ bien el lunes? (Does Monday suit you?)
questions.explain: Venir bien is a fixed expression meaning “to suit”.
